newsitem.title: CHINA: China launches war on rampant drugs crime.
newsitem.headline: China launches war on rampant drugs crime.

text.p: China has launched a campaign against rampant drugs crime, vowing to crack down on addicts, traffickers and local authorities that allow growers to tend their illegal crops, officials said on Tuesday.
A rising international tide of narcotics crime has helped create the most serious drugs crisis in China since the trade was all but wiped out in the early 1950s, the People's Daily said.

Beijing, which frequently executes drug traffickers, has ordered a nationwide campaign that will run until September. It will aim to curb drugs crimes through tougher legal action, expanded propaganda and tighter organisation, said the newspaper, mouthpiece of the ruling Communist Party.
"We must first make full use of all the weapons of the law to strike hard at criminal drugs activities and resolutely hold back their increasingly rampant spread," it said.

Some local officials did not realise the seriousness of the drugs crisis while others even approved of drugs production, the Xinhua news agency quoted the National Committee of Narcotics Control as saying.
"It was discovered that some grassroots-level authorities have privately given the green light to drug growers, which has stimulated the spread of drug production and use," it said.
The anti-drugs campaign will be combined with China's "Strike Hard" war on crime, which had already targeted drugs offences, a narcotics commitee official told Reuters.

China's communists ended centuries of widespread drugs use in the years after their 1949 revolution, but they have seen the trade in heroin, opium and illegal stimulants surge back as economic reforms have loosened once-strict social controls.
More open borders have allowed drugs to flow across China from the "Golden Triangle" opium growing region that straddles parts of Burma, Thailand and Laos and on to markets in the West.

Increasing urban affluence has turned coastal cities into new centres of demand, while thousands of surplus rural labourers have become hooked on drugs either smuggled into the country or grown on the remote and temperate hills of southwest China.
By the end of 1995, officials had registered 520,000 illegal drug users in 1,600 towns and counties, the People's Daily said.

Each Chinese province, region and main city and all areas with serious narcotics problems should set up rehabilitation centres and mobilise officials, social organisations and families to assist in weaning addicts off drugs, it said.
Mass involvement was crucial, but if the war on drugs could be won in the 1950s it could be won again.
"After liberation (in 1949) our national power was far less than now, we had less money and our equipment was less advanced -- yet the battle against drugs was fought most beautifully," it said.
Close ties between the Communist Party and populace would be China's "secret weapon" in the campaign, it said.
Government and party leaders at all levels should focus on drugs control, boost cooperation and avoid inter-departmental wrangling, the narcotics committee said.
Public trials for drug offenders should be encouraged, penalties should strictly accord with the law and fines should never be levied in place of harsher punishment, it said.
